items.name: SAT
items.tip: Take a full timed practice test in Bluebook first to find your weak areas. Drill those in the official question bank, then retake a full test every 2–3 weeks and review every miss.
steps: Take a full practice test in Bluebook to get a baseline score and see which skills cost you the most points.
2–3 times a week: drill your weakest skills in the official question bank or Khan Academy, about 30–45 minutes each.
Every 2–3 weeks: take another full practice test. Review every missed question until you could explain the right answer to a friend.
Register at least 3 weeks early; most students take it twice (junior spring and senior fall).

items.name: ACT
items.tip: Pacing is the hardest part of the ACT. Take official practice tests under real time limits and learn to skip and come back. Science is about reading graphs, not memorizing facts.
steps: Take a free official ACT practice test under real time limits. The ACT is about pacing more than hard content.
Practice by section: learn the common grammar rules for English, review algebra and geometry for Math, and for Science practice reading graphs quickly.
Retake a timed section every week and track your time per question. Skip and come back when you're stuck.
Register by the regular deadline to avoid late fees; many students test in junior spring and again senior fall.

items.name: CLEP exams

Book the exam at a test center or online once your practice scores are solid.

steps: Daily: 15–20 minutes of listening (podcasts, shows, music) and speaking out loud. The exam rewards communicating, not perfect grammar.
Weekly: practice one task type under exam timing, such as the email reply, argumentative essay, conversation, or cultural comparison. Record yourself for the speaking ones.
Last 4 weeks: past free-response prompts from AP Students, scored with the official guidelines. Learn a few transition phrases you can use in every task.

items.name: AP Spanish Literature and Culture
items.tip: Know every work on the required reading list: author, period, themes. Practice comparing texts in Spanish under time limits.
steps: Every week: learn the unit from your class or the videos below, then do practice questions on it the same week. Small, regular reviews beat cramming.
From March: take one full timed practice exam. Write down why you missed each question (content, misread, or ran out of time) and fix the biggest pattern.
Last 4 weeks: do past free-response questions from AP Students under time limits and grade them with the official scoring guidelines. This is the single best use of your time.

items.name: AP 2-D Art and Design
items.tip: There's no exam. Your portfolio is the score. Pick a sustained investigation question early, document your process, and study scored sample portfolios.
steps: Pick your sustained investigation question early (fall) and make work regularly. Volume plus visible growth is what scorers look for.
Document your process: photos, sketches and short notes on how each piece connects to your question.
Study scored sample portfolios on AP Students, then edit your written statements to match what high scorers do.

items.name: AP Seminar
items.tip: Most of the score comes from team and individual performance tasks during the year. Practice evaluating source credibility and building arguments from multiple perspectives.
steps: Start the performance tasks early. Most of the score is project work done during the year, not one exam day.
Practice judging sources: who wrote it, what evidence it uses, and what perspective it leaves out.
Read high-scoring samples on AP Students and outline your work against the official rubric before writing.
